question.text: The COMPANY form is the least-used constitutional option for an Indian AIF. Which reason BEST explains this?

answer.text: Companies Act, 2013 restricts a private company's private placements to not more than 200 investors, whereas AIF Regulations permit up to 1,000 investors per scheme; plus corporate governance/compliance is cumbersome
A company cannot legally appoint an investment manager
Companies are prohibited by SEBI from registering as an AIF
A company cannot have a custodian or fund administrator

explanation.text: **The Logic:** Two problems make the company form least-preferred: (1) Section 42 of Companies Act, 2013 caps private placement at 200 investors per issue, but AIF Regulations allow up to 1,000 investors per scheme (excluding accredited investors) — so a company-AIF cannot use its full investor slot. (2) The governance and compliance burden under Companies Act is heavy compared to a trust. **The Trap:** Options B, C, and D are fabricated impossibilities. The company form is ALLOWED, just operationally inferior. The 200 vs 1,000 gap is the concrete regulatory limitation you need to know. **Cross-Exam Context:** Same concept in XIX-C, XIX-D. XIX-A/B distributors should note this when explaining why a particular fund is not offered in company form. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** If a Cat III fund is set up as a company, your investor-count headroom shrinks from 1,000 to 200 — that alone constrains capacity and AUM growth. Always pick trust if capacity matters.
